subject: Agriculture
topic: Growing Crops: From Seed to Harvest
content: Crop farming follows a general process. Land Preparation: clearing the land and turning the soil (ploughing) so seeds can be planted easily. Planting: putting seeds into the soil at the right depth and spacing, usually at the start of the rainy season for crops like maize. Weeding: removing unwanted plants (weeds) that compete with crops for water, sunlight, and nutrients. Watering/Irrigation: giving crops enough water, either from rain or by watering them directly. Applying Fertilizer: adding nutrients to help crops grow strong and healthy. Harvesting: picking or cutting the mature crop when it is ready. Common crops grown in Zimbabwe include maize (the staple food), groundnuts, sorghum, cotton, and vegetables like tomatoes and cabbages.

subject: Agriculture
content: Farmers keep animals (livestock) for food, income, and other uses. Common farm animals in Zimbabwe include cattle (for milk, meat, and draught power for ploughing), goats and sheep (for meat and milk), chickens (for eggs and meat), and pigs (for meat). Good animal care includes: providing clean water every day, giving proper feed (grass, grain, or special feed), keeping shelters clean and safe from predators, and taking animals for vaccinations and dipping (to control ticks) to prevent disease. Healthy, well-cared-for animals grow faster and provide better products for the farmer.

subject: Agriculture
topic: Starting a School or Home Garden
content: A garden is a small piece of land used to grow vegetables, fruits, or flowers. Steps to start a simple garden: choose a sunny spot with good soil, clear the ground of weeds and stones, dig and loosen the soil, make beds or rows, plant seeds or seedlings at the correct spacing, water regularly, and remove weeds as they appear. Common vegetables grown in home and school gardens in Zimbabwe include rape, covo, tomatoes, onions, and carrots. Gardens can provide fresh, healthy food for a family or school and can also be sold for extra income.

subject: ICT/Computer Studies
content: A computer is a machine that can store and process information. The main parts include: the Monitor (screen that displays information), the Keyboard (used to type letters and numbers), the Mouse (used to point, click, and select things on the screen), the CPU/System Unit (the 'brain' of the computer that processes information, usually a box-shaped case), and Speakers (produce sound). Hardware refers to the physical parts you can touch, like the keyboard and monitor. Software refers to the programs that run on the computer, like a word processor or a game, which you cannot physically touch.

subject: ICT/Computer Studies
topic: Uses of ICT and Staying Safe Online
content: Information and Communication Technology (ICT) is used in daily life for communication (phone calls, messages, video calls), learning (educational apps and websites), entertainment (games, videos, music), and work (typing documents, doing calculations). Staying safe online is very important. Rules for internet safety include: never share your full name, address, or school with strangers online, tell a trusted adult if someone online makes you uncomfortable, never meet in person with someone you only know from the internet, use strong passwords and don't share them, and take breaks from screens to protect your eyes and health.

subject: Family, Religious and Moral Education
content: Zimbabwe is home to people of many different religions who live together peacefully. Christianity is the most widely followed religion, based on the teachings of Jesus Christ, with believers attending church and reading the Bible. African Traditional Religion involves belief in a Supreme Being (like Mwari in Shona belief) and respect for ancestors (Vadzimu), often through ceremonies. Islam is followed by a smaller number of Zimbabweans, based on the teachings of the Quran and the Prophet Muhammad. Other religions practiced in Zimbabwe include Hinduism and Judaism, among smaller communities. Learning about different religions helps us respect and understand people who believe differently from us.
source: ZIMSEC Primary Family, Religious and Moral Education

subject: Family, Religious and Moral Education
content: Moral values guide us to do what is right. Important values taught in Zimbabwean schools include: Honesty (telling the truth and not stealing or cheating), Respect (treating others, especially elders and teachers, with courtesy), Responsibility (completing your duties and owning up to your mistakes), Kindness (helping others and being considerate of their feelings), Discipline (following rules and controlling your behaviour), and Hard Work (putting in effort at school, home, and in the community). Practicing these values every day, at home, at school, and in the community, helps build good character and a peaceful society.
source: ZIMSEC Primary Family, Religious and Moral Education

subject: Family, Religious and Moral Education
topic: Personal Hygiene and Good Health Habits
content: Good personal hygiene helps keep you healthy and prevents illness. Daily hygiene habits include: bathing every day, brushing teeth twice a day (morning and night), washing hands with soap before eating and after using the toilet, wearing clean clothes, keeping fingernails short and clean, and covering your mouth when coughing or sneezing. Good health habits also include eating a balanced diet with fruits and vegetables, drinking clean water, getting enough sleep (about 9-11 hours for children), and exercising regularly. These habits help prevent the spread of germs and diseases like diarrhoea and colds.
source: ZIMSEC Primary Family, Religious and Moral Education

subject: Physical Education
content: Physical Education (PE) helps children develop strong, healthy bodies and good coordination. Benefits of regular exercise include: a stronger heart and lungs, stronger muscles and bones, healthy body weight, better sleep, improved mood and reduced stress, and better concentration in class. Common PE activities in Zimbabwean schools include running, jumping, stretching exercises, ball games, and simple gymnastics. Children should aim for at least 60 minutes of physical activity most days. Always warm up with light stretching before exercising and cool down afterward to avoid injury.

subject: Physical Education
topic: Common Games and Sports in Zimbabwean Schools
content: Zimbabwean primary schools play many traditional and modern games and sports. Popular sports include football (soccer), netball (very popular among girls), athletics (running races, long jump, high jump), and volleyball. Traditional games include Nhodo (a stone-throwing and catching game), Tsoro (a traditional board game using seeds or stones), and skipping rope games, often accompanied by singing. Playing games and sports teaches teamwork, following rules, fair play, and healthy competition, alongside the physical benefits of being active.

subject: Art and Music
content: Zimbabwe has a rich tradition of music. The Mbira (thumb piano) is one of the most important traditional instruments, made of metal keys attached to a wooden board, often played inside a resonator called a 'deze' (calabash gourd), and is central to Shona spiritual and cultural ceremonies. Ngoma (drums) are used to keep rhythm in traditional dances and ceremonies. Hosho are shakers made from dried gourds filled with seeds, played alongside the mbira to keep the beat. Traditional music often accompanies storytelling, ceremonies, and celebrations, and modern Zimbabwean music genres like Sungura and Chimurenga music have grown from these traditional roots.

subject: Art and Music
content: Zimbabwe is known for several traditional arts and crafts. Stone sculpture (Shona Sculpture) uses stones like serpentine and springstone to carve figures, often depicting people, animals, or spiritual themes, and is famous internationally. Basketry involves weaving baskets from natural materials like grass, reeds, or palm leaves, used for carrying and storing food. Pottery involves shaping clay into pots, bowls, and other containers, often used for cooking and storing water. Beadwork involves creating jewellery and decorations using colourful beads. These crafts are passed down through generations and are an important part of Zimbabwe's cultural heritage and economy.

subject: Mathematics
content: Length measures how long or tall something is, using units like millimetres (mm), centimetres (cm), metres (m), and kilometres (km). 100 cm = 1 m, and 1000 m = 1 km. Mass measures how heavy something is, using units like grams (g) and kilograms (kg). 1000 g = 1 kg. Capacity measures how much liquid something can hold, using units like millilitres (ml) and litres (l). 1000 ml = 1 litre. Choosing the right unit and tool matters: use a ruler for small lengths, a tape measure for longer distances, a scale for mass, and a measuring jug for liquids.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Data Handling: Tables, Charts, and Graphs
content: Data handling means collecting, organizing, and displaying information so it is easy to understand. A tally chart uses marks (usually grouped in fives) to count how many times something happens. A bar graph uses bars of different heights to compare amounts - taller bars mean bigger numbers. A pictograph uses pictures or symbols to represent data, where each picture might stand for a certain number of items. When reading any graph or chart, always check the title (what it's about) and the key or labels (what the numbers or symbols mean) before answering questions about it.

subject: Mathematics
content: Place value tells us what a digit in a number is worth based on its position. In the number 4,527: the 4 is in the thousands place (worth 4000), the 5 is in the hundreds place (worth 500), the 2 is in the tens place (worth 20), and the 7 is in the ones place (worth 7). Understanding place value helps with adding, subtracting, and comparing numbers correctly. Number patterns follow a rule, like counting in 2s (2, 4, 6, 8...), 5s (5, 10, 15, 20...), or 10s (10, 20, 30, 40...). Recognizing the rule in a pattern helps you predict the next numbers in a sequence.

subject: English Language
content: Punctuation marks help make writing clear and easy to read. A full stop (.) ends a statement sentence. A question mark (?) ends a question. An exclamation mark (!) shows strong feeling or emphasis. A comma (,) separates items in a list or adds a short pause in a sentence. A capital letter starts every sentence and every proper noun (names of specific people, places, and things, like 'Zimbabwe' or 'Tendai'). An apostrophe (') shows possession ('Tendai's book') or shows a letter has been left out in a contraction ('don't' = 'do not').

subject: English Language
content: A composition is a piece of writing on a given topic. Common types include: Narrative composition (tells a story with a beginning, middle, and end, often including characters and a problem to solve), Descriptive composition (describes a person, place, or thing in vivid detail using the five senses), and Letter writing (formal letters to authorities follow a specific layout with sender's address, date, and a formal closing; informal letters to friends or family are more relaxed in tone). Always plan your composition before writing, organize your ideas into paragraphs, and check your spelling and punctuation when you finish.

subject: English Language
content: A preposition shows the position or relationship of a noun to other words in a sentence, like in, on, under, behind, between, near, and above. Example: 'The book is on the table' - 'on' shows the position. A conjunction joins words, phrases, or sentences together, like and, but, or, because, and so. Example: 'I wanted to play, but it was raining' - 'but' joins the two ideas and shows contrast. Using prepositions and conjunctions correctly helps you write clearer, more connected sentences instead of many short, choppy ones.

subject: Environmental Science
content: A force is a push or a pull that can make an object start moving, stop moving, speed up, slow down, or change direction. Gravity is a force that pulls objects toward the Earth, which is why things fall down when dropped. Friction is a force that slows down movement when two surfaces rub against each other. Simple machines make work easier by changing the size or direction of a force needed. Examples include: the lever (like a seesaw or crowbar, used to lift heavy objects with less effort), the wheel and axle (like a wheelbarrow, helps move things more easily), the inclined plane (a ramp, makes it easier to move objects up to a height), and the pulley (a wheel with a rope, used to lift objects like a flag up a pole).

subject: Environmental Science
topic: Matter and Materials: Solids, Liquids, and Gases
content: Matter is anything that takes up space and has mass. Matter exists in three main states. Solids have a fixed shape and volume, and do not flow (e.g., a rock, a book, ice). Liquids have a fixed volume but take the shape of their container, and can flow (e.g., water, milk, oil). Gases have no fixed shape or volume, spread out to fill any container, and are usually invisible (e.g., air, steam, oxygen). Matter can change from one state to another: water freezes into ice (liquid to solid), ice melts into water (solid to liquid), and water boils into steam (liquid to gas), usually caused by changes in temperature.

subject: Environmental Science
topic: Natural Disasters and Safety in Zimbabwe
content: Natural disasters are extreme events in nature that can cause damage and harm. Zimbabwe is affected mainly by droughts (long periods without enough rain, harming crops and water supplies) and floods (heavy rains causing rivers to overflow, damaging homes and roads, sometimes worsened by cyclones like Cyclone Idai in 2019, which caused severe damage in Manicaland province). Veld fires (uncontrolled bushfires, common in the dry season) are also a risk. Safety measures include: listening to weather warnings from local authorities, avoiding building homes near riverbanks in flood-prone areas, conserving water during droughts, and never leaving fires unattended in dry grassland.
